l6: MIA is usually the best choice for South Beach and central Miami Beach. For Bal Harbour, Surfside, and the northern end of Miami Beach, compare MIA and FLL based on arrival time, airfare, and traffic conditions.
l7: Is MIA or FLL better for Aventura?

l9: Is FLL better than MIA for Sunny Isles?
l10: In most cases, yes. FLL is normally the more convenient airport for Sunny Isles. The final drive can still slow near coastal roads, especially during peak periods.
l11: Which airport is closest to Boca Raton?

l14: Use MIA for PortMiami and FLL for Port Everglades whenever the flight schedule allows. Avoid booking an arrival with little margin before cruise check-in.

l17: DJT (Palm Beach) vs. FLL — which should I fly into?
l18: It depends on where you're headed. DJT is the better choice for Palm Beach, West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, and Boca Raton. FLL is the stronger option for Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood, Aventura, Sunny Isles, and points south. The two airports sit about 50 miles apart — roughly an hour's drive — so a nonstop into the 'wrong' one to save on airfare can add more time than it saves. Compare against your final destination, not just fare.
l19: Which airport is closest to Hallandale Beach, Florida?
l20: FLL is normally the closest major commercial airport to Hallandale Beach. MIA is farther south and DJT is much farther north.
l21: Which airport is nearest to Boynton Beach, Florida?
l22: DJT (formerly PBI) is normally the nearest major commercial airport to Boynton Beach. FLL is the next airport to compare when its flight schedule or fare is better.
l23: Is Fort Lauderdale Airport the same as Miami Airport?
l24: No. Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) and Miami International Airport (MIA) are two separate airports in two different counties, roughly 26 to 37 road miles apart depending on route. Booking sites sometimes group them together in search results because both serve the greater Miami area, but they have different codes, terminals, and ground transportation.
l25: How far is DJT (Palm Beach) from FLL?
l26: Roughly 45 to 50 road miles, depending on route, which is normally about an hour's drive. For destinations near the Broward-Palm Beach county line, compare both airports' flight schedules before assuming the closer one wins.

h4: MIA, FLL, or DJT — which one, really?
h5: The cheapest ticket isn't always the fastest trip. In South Florida, the right airport can save more time than the right flight — once baggage claim, terminal walking, I-95 traffic, and the final drive are counted.
h6: Miami International (MIA), Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International (FLL), and Palm Beach's airport serve one continuous metro region, but they are not interchangeable. A traveler staying in Brickell may save time paying slightly more for a flight into MIA. A family headed to Aventura may land closer to their destination at FLL. A passenger bound for Palm Beach could lose over an hour by defaulting to Miami simply because "Miami" is in the name.
h7: This guide compares the three from the perspective that matters after the aircraft door opens: how quickly and comfortably you reach your actual destination.
h8: 2026 naming update: Palm Beach International Airport was officially renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport on July 9, 2026, and its passenger-facing IATA code changed from PBI to DJT on August 18, 2026. Some airlines and booking sites may still show PBI — search either code for flights.
h9: How far apart are the airports themselves? MIA to FLL is roughly 26–37 road miles depending on route and exact addresses, normally 30–60 minutes depending on traffic. FLL to DJT is roughly 45–50 road miles, normally 50–80 minutes depending on traffic. MIA to DJT is roughly 70–75 road miles, normally 75 minutes to 2 hours depending on traffic. These are route-planning ranges, not straight-line distances, and not a substitute for checking conditions on the day — during commuter traffic, flying into the "wrong" one to save on airfare can add an hour or more once the drive is counted.
h10: Methodology: ranges above are road-distance estimates between the airports themselves. Destination-specific mile and time ranges in the table below are approximate and vary by the exact address, time of day, and traffic — treat every figure here as a planning range, not a quote.

h43: These are geographic starting points, not guarantees — traffic, weather, construction, events, and airline schedules can change the result.
h46: South Florida's primary international gateway and the airport with the broadest global reach — usually the natural choice for travelers from Latin America, the Caribbean, and many long-haul markets, plus anyone headed to central or southern Miami-Dade.
h47: Its strength is flight selection. Its tradeoff is scale: three terminal areas (North, Central, South) spread across six concourses — D, E, F, G, H, and J. Concourse D alone runs a full mile end to end. A flight-tracked chauffeur earns its keep here — see MIA airport transfers for how Onyx handles the pickup.
h48: Best for: Brickell, Downtown Miami, Coral Gables, Coconut Grove, Key Biscayne, Doral, South Miami, Kendall, the Florida Keys, and usually PortMiami and South Beach.
h50: "Arrived" isn't the same as "curbside." International passengers still taxi to the gate, walk to immigration, clear passport control, collect baggage, and pass customs. Even a domestic flight with a checked bag adds real time.
h51: Onyx tip: for an international arrival, send the flight number and confirm if you're checking bags — "landed" and "ready for pickup" can be very different moments.
h54: Often called the smaller alternative to MIA — but for northern Miami-Dade and Broward, it's frequently not the alternative, it's the better airport. Four terminals, 66 gates, generally an easier layout than MIA. See FLL airport transfers for pickup details.
h55: Best for: Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood, Dania Beach, Hallandale Beach, Aventura, Sunny Isles Beach, Golden Beach, much of northern Miami Beach, and Port Everglades.
h56: A slightly higher fare into FLL can be worth it if it removes a long central-Miami transfer — especially for families, tired travelers, and anyone with a meeting soon after landing. For Brickell, Coral Gables, or the Keys, though, the southbound drive can erase that advantage.
h58: Palm Beach / President Donald J. Trump International (DJT, formerly PBI)
h59: Palm Beach County's main commercial airport, and the most compact terminal experience of the three — one building, three concourses (A, B, C), with gates on Level 2 and ground transportation and baggage claim one floor down on Level 1. Officially renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport as of July 9, 2026 — the passenger code changed from PBI to DJT on August 18, 2026. See DJT / Palm Beach airport transfers for pickup details.
h60: Best for: West Palm Beach, Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Wellington, Delray Beach, and Boca Raton when the flight schedule works.
h61: The tradeoff: fewer routes than MIA or FLL. A connection added just to use the closest airport can take longer than a nonstop into FLL plus a ground transfer — weigh both sides of the trip.
h63: Where you'll actually meet your ride
h64: Airport size drives pickup time more than anything else. MIA is the largest of the three by a wide margin — multiple concourses, several ground transportation doors, and a longer walk from most gates to the curb. FLL's footprint is smaller. That difference alone accounts for most of the gap below.
h66: Based on Onyx trip records for gate-to-curb walking time. Ground transportation is on Level 1 for most concourses. Rideshare apps typically assign pickups across Level 1 (Arrivals) and Level 2 (Departures) curbs — prearranged chauffeur pickup uses its own confirmed curb location, which is not always the same door, so confirm the meeting point at booking rather than assuming it matches a rideshare pin.
h68: Based on Onyx trip records — typically faster than MIA, largely a function of the smaller terminal footprint. Note: the rideshare zones below are Uber/Lyft pickup points, not the Onyx pickup location — a licensed prearranged chauffeur meets you curbside or at an agreed terminal point confirmed at booking, which is not always the same as the rideshare zone.
a3: Diagram of Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport rideshare pickup zones by terminal: Terminal 1 at Zone Z, Terminal 2 near GTA-2, and Terminals 3 and 4 through Zones A-D in the Palm Garage
h69: Shown for general orientation — these are the app-based rideshare zones, not the Onyx pickup point. Your chauffeur's meeting location is confirmed at booking.
h70: DJT pickup logistics: ground transportation is on Level 1 near baggage claim. The rideshare curb is one level up, on Level 3 — Departures; a prearranged chauffeur pickup point is confirmed separately at booking and may differ. Onyx trip volume through DJT isn't yet high enough to publish a reliable time range.
h73: Start with your exact address. "Miami" can mean Brickell, Aventura, or an address over an hour away — use the actual destination, not the city name.
h74: Compare arrival times. A flight landing before rush hour can beat one that saves $50 but arrives at 5:30pm.
h75: Price the entire trip. Airfare, bags, ground transportation, and added travel time — the cheapest ticket can create the most expensive day.
h76: Check nonstop vs. connection. A nearby airport isn't always better if it requires an extra connection.
h77: Account for baggage and mobility. Checked luggage, small children, and mobility limitations all raise the value of a shorter transfer.
h78: Protect time-sensitive plans. For cruises, meetings, or connections, choose the realistic buffer, not the optimistic map estimate.
h81: South Florida's three airports sit along a north-south corridor, but transfers don't happen on an empty map. I-95 congestion, lane closures, rain, cruise traffic, and events can all change the journey. Beach destinations add a final bottleneck: a hotel can look close in a straight line while still requiring a slow run through a limited number of causeways.
h84: A flight can show "arrived" while still taxiing. After that: gate, immigration, baggage, customs, and the walk out. Professional pickup uses flight tracking plus direct communication with the passenger — not just a landing alert.
h87: Choose MIA for the widest international network and most trips to Brickell, Downtown Miami, Coral Gables, Coconut Grove, South Miami, PortMiami, and the Florida Keys.
h88: Choose FLL for Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood, Port Everglades, Aventura, Sunny Isles, and many trips to Bal Harbour or northern Miami Beach.
h89: Choose DJT for Palm Beach, West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Delray Beach, and often Boca Raton when its schedule is competitive.
h90: The rule that matters most: don't choose an airport by city name alone. Compare the complete journey from departure to the exact door of your South Florida destination.
